comparator.name: Dutch Language and Culture
comparator.sourceNotes: The current 2026–27 Leiden study product accounts for 180 EC: a 60-EC first-year core, 30 EC of second-year compulsory work, 50 EC of internal specialisation study spanning years two and three, a 10-EC bachelor thesis and 30 EC open elective space. The Dutch Linguistics specialisation group is instantiated because it most directly preserves the programme’s broad Dutch-language identity; its two 10-EC compulsory courses and the first three eligible 10-EC listed choices make the required 50 EC. This choice is made independently of UCR fit. The 0-EC mentoring and thesis-seminar modules are omitted. The 2026–27 programme-specific OER states that formal graduation directions are not applicable, so routeSelection is null even though the study product organises the 50-EC bound-choice space into internal specialisation groups. The fixed-queue reassessment on 2026-10-16 preserves every settled external component and credit weight and the neutral internal Dutch Linguistics choice. The current programme page and 2026–27 OER were rechecked: rhetoric, stylistics, literary interpretation and language/media relations are substantive parts of the target, while formal graduation directions remain inapplicable. Media is integrated into the four disciplinary areas rather than presented as a separate current specialisation.

core: Dutch language structure, historical and social variation, cognition and empirical linguistic research
Language use, argumentation, stylistics, persuasion and communication in social settings
Older and modern Dutch literature, literary interpretation, cultural history and international connections
Relations between language, literature and media, including digital texts and cultural representation
Linguistic and literary research methods and a Dutch Studies thesis
adjacent: Language, cognition, persuasion and mediated public communication
Literary meaning across historical contexts, narrative forms and media
questions: How do linguistic choices, arguments and mediated narratives influence understanding and public judgment?
How do texts and media represent migration, racism, climate and cultural change?

Dutch structural, historical and social linguistics

alternatives.label: Language, persuasion, cognition & media
alternatives.labelReason: Five communication, four literature and five media courses form the central textual/communicative study. Five psychology/cognition/methods and four sociology courses examine processing, influence and public discourse. The label reflects those weights and makes no Dutch-specialist claim.
alternatives.concept: Study how language, arguments and narratives create meaning and influence people, combining rhetoric and stylistics with literary and media analysis, language processing, social psychology and empirical social inquiry. The programme approaches the target through related fields; it does not provide Dutch structural linguistics or a Dutch literary-period sequence.
progression: Introductory rhetoric, literary interpretation, film and sociology precede their advanced applications. Brain & Behavior in semester 2 precedes Higher Order Functions in semester 3 and Psycholinguistics in semester 6. Modern Sociology in semester 3 precedes Contemporary Social Theory in semester 5. Rhetoric precedes local school practice and institutional persuasive communication. Formal prerequisites and all exact planned terms pass.

alternatives.label: Literature, cultural history & media
alternatives.labelReason: Six literature, six media, four communication, three history, two art/museum and two sociology courses give the programme a predominantly literary and cultural organising logic. The two visual-art courses are complementary study of cultural representation and display, not Dutch art-history coverage.
alternatives.concept: Interpret literary texts and their circulation through film, documentary, material media and creative practice, with historical source work and focused study of cultural representation, museums and social questions. This related cultural programme does not reproduce older or modern Dutch literature or Dutch-language primary-source training.
alternatives.distinctness: Nine courses / 67.5 EC differ in each direction. The second programme removes the cognitive/psychological sequence, rhetoric teaching, institutional persuasion and advanced sociological theory. It adds myth and life writing, environmental media/communication, art and museum interpretation, modern/imperial history and local primary-source research. These are curricular consequences of historical literary and cultural interpretation, rather than a relabelled persuasion programme.
progression: Introductory literature, rhetoric, film and sociology come first. Western Art History precedes Modern Art & Modern Museums; Modern History precedes History of Empires and the Walcheren primary-source seminar. Introductory media and literary work precede adaptation, literary research, documentary and creative communication. Every formal prerequisite and exact planned term passes.

selection.assessment: Two complete and substantively different related programmes are accepted in sequence. A third direction in Dutch structural/historical/social linguistics cannot form a complete 24-course programme: Psycholinguistics addresses acquisition and processing and Style & Meaning addresses textual choices, but neither supplies Dutch phonology, morphology, syntax, historical variation or a sustained sociolinguistics sequence. Introductory Dutch teaches everyday communication rather than academic Dutch analysis. Digital corpora is support-only evidence, not an independently generating direction; a technical data-science programme would add unevidenced priorities, while another media/communication version would repeat the accepted routes. The historical no-match overstated the necessity of full disciplinary equivalence.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: directly teaches rhetorical analysis and the construction of written and spoken arguments, providing the foundation for analysing persuasive language
directly develops practical criticism, genre analysis and literary interpretation across fiction, poetry, drama and non-fiction
provides formal film analysis and historically situated study of narrative, cinematography, editing and sound as cultural meaning-making
introduces race, gender, institutions and socially situated interpretation, supporting specified analysis of whose language and narratives acquire cultural authority
provides the required foundations in neural communication, brain anatomy, psychological theories and research approaches before advanced language processing and cognition
directly studies stylistics, showing how phonetic, discoursal and cognitive linguistic choices create interpretive effects, especially in literary texts

investigates literary forms and representations of identity, responsibility and community chronologically from Gilgamesh to postmodernity; it supplies comparative literary history, not Dutch period coverage
examines modern social theory in imperial and colonial contexts, supplying the theoretical foundations for analysing the institutions and inequalities within which public discourse operates
examines early printed books and other material media as evidence of how technologies shape communication, cultural memory and knowledge circulation
teaches regression, factor analysis, analysis of variance and other multivariate models for analysing empirical relations among psychological variables in language and persuasion research

studies memory, attention, social cognition and decision-making together with experimental approaches, giving a specific complementary account of the processes on which understanding and persuasive judgment depend

applies public-speaking, debating and storytelling theory in designed exercises with local primary-school children, principally in Dutch; this is applied rhetoric rather than Dutch-teacher qualification
analyses American media narratives, including Indigenous and disability representation, to investigate how storytelling distributes cultural authority; it does not teach Dutch media history
examines how the presence of others influences thoughts, feelings and behaviour, providing a specific account of audience and social influence alongside rhetorical persuasion
teaches qualitative research design, data collection, interpretation and reflexivity for studying meaning-making and communication in social settings
directly examines framing, nudging, cognitive shortcuts and persuasion ethics, then applies them to communication problems of local institutions
directly investigates literary-to-film adaptation, intertextuality and the formal analysis of narrative in texts and screen media
examines race, power, resistance and erasure through American film, photography and music, providing specified analysis of racism and representation rather than Dutch regional content

investigates Habermas, Fraser and the public/civil sphere, solidarity and migrant representation through theory and an empirical civil-society project; this is public-discourse inquiry rather than Dutch sociolinguistics
combines close reading with poetry, rhythm, voice, performance and reflective creative projects to investigate how language and media produce meaning
applies humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic perspectives in a literary research project; these are interpretive methods rather than a Dutch literature sequence
combines historical/ethical analysis of documentary representations with a researched presentation, short documentary and analytical writing
directly studies language acquisition, production, comprehension, semantics, bilingualism and experimental language research; it is not Dutch structural or historical linguistics
directly analyses environmental narratives, images, sound and postcolonial media, pursuing the target’s explicit question of how cultural texts interpret climate and global issues
examines industrialisation, political ideologies, war, decolonisation and welfare states as specified historical processes shaping the modern texts and cultural narratives studied in the programme

develops visual analysis of European and American art from the Renaissance onward and examines how institutions and critics establish cultural meaning; this complements analysis of the visual media into which texts circulate

examines the transmission of myths and narratives between ancient, Indian, Byzantine and Arabic literary traditions and into visual/oral forms, providing a specified comparative method for international literary connections
analyses memoirs, diaries, travel narrative, autobiography and blogs as forms of literary self-representation and develops original narrative work
analyses arguments, slogans, protest art and social media in climate debate, a specific application of the target’s language-influence and literary climate questions
studies empire, power and imperial change, providing a specific historical complement to postcolonial literary interpretation and mediated cultural authority
examines how museum display and curatorial choices shape the public interpretation of modern art, providing a focused complement on the institutional mediation of cultural meaning

researches the 1809 Walcheren expedition through Dutch, French and British diaries, letters and reports, adding concrete historical source work connected with the target’s Dutch/international cultural-history interests
blocks: Both directly teach argumentation and persuasion; the UCR rhetoric foundation is not Dutch-language proficiency study.
Both examine how linguistic choices produce interpretive and rhetorical effects. UCR stylistics does not supply Dutch-specific linguistic progression.
Both concern strategic persuasive communication. UCR directly applies framing and persuasion to institutional communication problems, without reproducing Dutch-specialist study.
Both directly teach literary analysis and interpretation. UCR uses multiple literary traditions rather than a Dutch textual corpus.
Both directly investigate theoretical approaches to interpreting literature. The UCR project is not a Dutch literary-period sequence.

notes.text: Leiden offers a Dutch-language disciplinary curriculum in historical and modern Dutch literature, Dutch structural and social linguistics, rhetoric, media and Dutch Studies research. These UCR programmes pursue related questions through rhetoric, stylistics, literature, media, cognition and cultural history. They do not reproduce Dutch phonology, morphology, syntax, historical language, a Dutch literary-period sequence, or the required Dutch-linguistics thesis.
